```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: true
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
walk  <- load_walk()  |> arrange(id, month)
clear <- load_clear() |> arrange(id, week)
diary <- load_diary() |> arrange(id, period)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulated data"}
All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
:::

These exercises practise the skills of Module 7: fitting GEE with `geepack::geeglm()` to continuous, binary and count outcomes, choosing and comparing working correlations, distinguishing model-based from robust (sandwich) standard errors, recognising the small-sample problem of the sandwich, and correcting GEE for dropout with inverse-probability weights. Code chunks contain blanks (`___`) and are set to `eval: false` so that the workbook renders before you complete them. Change them to `eval: true`, or run them interactively, once the blanks are filled.

Notice that the setup chunk sorts every dataset by participant and time. `geeglm()` treats consecutive rows with the same identifier as one cluster, so this matters. Pass identifiers as `factor(id)`: the course identifiers are character strings, which `geeglm()` cannot use directly.

The next chunk defines a function that computes the sandwich variance by hand, with an optional Mancl–DeRouen small-sample correction. It is the function from the notes; run it before Exercises 3, 5 and 9.

```{r}
#| label: helper
sandwich_gee <- function(fit, correction = c("none", "MD")) {
  correction <- match.arg(correction)
  X <- model.matrix(fit); y <- fit$y; mu <- fitted(fit)
  fam <- family(fit); eta <- fit$linear.predictors
  w <- fit$prior.weights; if (is.null(w)) w <- rep(1, length(y))
  alpha <- fit$geese$alpha
  cl <- split(seq_along(y), fit$id)
  p <- ncol(X); B <- matrix(0, p, p); parts <- vector("list", length(cl))
  for (k in seq_along(cl)) {
    r <- cl[[k]]; n <- length(r); R <- diag(n)
    if (fit$corstr == "exchangeable" && n > 1) { R[] <- alpha; diag(R) <- 1 }
    if (fit$corstr == "ar1" && n > 1) R <- alpha^abs(outer(1:n, 1:n, "-"))
    A <- diag(sqrt(fam$variance(mu[r]) / w[r]), n)
    Vinv <- solve(A %*% R %*% A)
    D <- fam$mu.eta(eta[r]) * X[r, , drop = FALSE]
    B <- B + t(D) %*% Vinv %*% D
    parts[[k]] <- list(D = D, Vinv = Vinv, e = y[r] - mu[r])
  }
  Binv <- solve(B); M <- matrix(0, p, p)
  for (pk in parts) {
    e <- pk$e
    if (correction == "MD") {
      H <- pk$D %*% Binv %*% t(pk$D) %*% pk$Vinv
      e <- solve(diag(nrow(H)) - H, e)
    }
    u <- t(pk$D) %*% pk$Vinv %*% e
    M <- M + u %*% t(u)
  }
  V <- Binv %*% M %*% Binv
  dimnames(V) <- list(colnames(X), colnames(X)); V
}
```

## Guided exercises

### Exercise 1. A GEE for WALK (LO 7.1, 7.4)

(a) Fit a Gaussian GEE to systolic blood pressure with a separate mean for each arm at each scheduled visit and an exchangeable working correlation.

```{r}
#| eval: false
gee_walk <- geeglm(sbp ~ ___ * arm, id = ___, waves = visit,
                   data = walk, family = gaussian, corstr = "___")
summary(gee_walk)
```

(b) Find in the output the estimated working correlation, the scale parameter and the number of clusters. What does the scale parameter represent for a Gaussian GEE?

(c) Use `emmeans` to estimate the difference in mean change from baseline to month 12 between each programme and usual care, with 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| eval: false
emm_walk <- emmeans(gee_walk, ~ visit_f | arm)
chg <- contrast(emm_walk, list(change_m12 = c(___, 0, 0, 0, 0, ___)))
confint(contrast(chg, "trt.vs.ctrl", by = NULL), adjust = "none")
```

(d) Which coefficients of the model equal these differences? Why?

(e) In one or two sentences, interpret the EP result as a population-average effect.

### Exercise 2. Working correlations and two kinds of standard error (LO 7.2, 7.3)

(a) Refit the model of Exercise 1 with `"independence"` and `"ar1"` working correlations.

```{r}
#| eval: false
cs <- c("independence", "exchangeable", "ar1")
fits <- lapply(cs, function(s) geeglm(sbp ~ visit_f * arm, id = factor(id),
                                      waves = ___, data = walk, corstr = s))
names(fits) <- cs
```

(b) For `visit_f12:armEP`, tabulate the estimate, the robust SE (`vcov(fit)`) and the model-based SE (`fit$geese$vbeta.naiv`) for each structure.

```{r}
#| eval: false
k <- "visit_f12:armEP"
data.frame(corstr = cs,
           estimate = sapply(fits, function(f) coef(f)[k]),
           se_robust = sapply(fits, function(f) sqrt(diag(vcov(f)))[k]),
           se_model = sapply(fits, function(f) sqrt(diag(f$geese$___))[18]))
```

(c) Why are the estimates under exchangeable and AR(1) so similar? Why is the robust SE larger under independence?

(d) Under independence the model-based SE is much larger than the robust SE. Explain why in terms of what the independence model "believes" about the data.

(e) Compute `QIC()` for the three fits. Does the structure with the smallest QIC seem sensible? What would you use to choose the working correlation instead?

### Exercise 3. A binary outcome: CLEAR (LO 7.1, 7.3, 7.4)

(a) Fit a logistic GEE for `itch` with `week * arm` and an exchangeable working correlation.

```{r}
#| eval: false
gee_clear <- geeglm(itch ~ week * arm, id = factor(id), waves = visit,
                    data = clear, family = ___, corstr = "exchangeable")
fixef_table(gee_clear, exponentiate = ___)
```

(b) Interpret `exp(week)` and `exp(week:armActive)`. What is the odds ratio comparing active with placebo at week 12, assuming equal odds at baseline?

(c) Estimate the proportion with itch in each arm at weeks 0 and 12, and the risk difference at week 12.

```{r}
#| eval: false
emmeans(gee_clear, ~ arm | week, at = list(week = c(0, 12)), type = "___")
confint(contrast(regrid(emmeans(gee_clear, ~ arm | week, at = list(week = 12))),
                 "___"))
```

(d) Compare the model-based, robust and Mancl–DeRouen standard errors (use `sandwich_gee(gee_clear, "MD")`). Are they close? What does that tell you about the working correlation?

### Exercise 4. A count outcome with exposure: DIARY (LO 7.4)

(a) Fit a Poisson GEE for `migraine_days` with `post * arm`, an exchangeable working correlation and an offset for the number of diary days.

```{r}
#| eval: false
gee_diary <- geeglm(migraine_days ~ post * arm + ___,
                    id = factor(id), waves = period + 1, data = diary,
                    family = poisson, corstr = "exchangeable")
```

(b) Which coefficient is the treatment effect? Give it as a rate ratio with a 95% CI and interpret it.

(c) Estimate the expected number of migraine days per 28 days in each arm before and after baseline.

```{r}
#| eval: false
emmeans(gee_diary, ~ arm | post, offset = ___, type = "response")
```

(d) The estimated scale parameter is well above 1. Does this invalidate the analysis? Explain.

### Exercise 5. How many clusters? (LO 7.5)

(a) The function below simulates one dataset with `n_clusters` clusters (half active), fits an exchangeable GEE and returns the estimate of the time-by-arm interaction (true value −0.5) and its sandwich and Mancl–DeRouen SEs. Complete it.

```{r}
#| eval: false
sim_one <- function(n_clusters) {
  d <- expand.grid(time = 0:4, id = seq_len(n_clusters))
  d$active <- as.integer(d$id > n_clusters / 2)
  b0 <- rnorm(n_clusters, 0, 2); b1 <- rnorm(n_clusters, 0, 0.5)
  d$y <- -0.5 * d$time - 0.5 * d$active * d$time +
    b0[d$id] + b1[d$id] * d$time + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 1.5)
  fit <- geeglm(y ~ time * active, id = id, data = d, corstr = "___")
  k <- "time:active"
  c(est = unname(coef(fit)[k]), se_sw = sqrt(vcov(fit)[k, k]),
    se_md = sqrt(sandwich_gee(fit, "___")[k, k]))
}
```

(b) Run 200 replications for 10 and for 40 clusters. For each, compute the empirical SD of the estimates, the mean of each SE and the coverage of 95% Wald intervals.

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1)
res <- lapply(c(10, 40), function(N) data.frame(N = N, t(replicate(___, sim_one(N)))))
res <- bind_rows(res)
res |> group_by(N) |>
  summarise(emp_sd = sd(est), se_sw = mean(se_sw), se_md = mean(se_md),
            cover_sw = mean(abs(est + 0.5) <= 1.96 * se_sw),
            cover_md = mean(abs(est + 0.5) <= 1.96 * se_md))
```

(c) Compute the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage estimate with 200 replications. Which of your differences are larger than Monte Carlo error?

(d) Summarise in two sentences what the simulation shows about the sandwich with few clusters.

### Exercise 6. Weighted GEE for dropout in CLEAR (LO 7.6) <span class="advanced-tag">ADVANCED</span>

(a) Build a "risk set" with one row for each participant and each visit from 2 up to and including the visit at which they dropped out. Record whether they stayed (`stay`) and their last observed severity before that visit (`prev_sev`).

```{r}
#| eval: false
grid <- clear |> distinct(id, arm) |> crossing(visit = 1:6) |>
  left_join(select(clear, id, visit, severity), by = c("id", "visit")) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(last_visit = max(visit[!is.na(severity)]), last_sev = severity) |>
  tidyr::fill(last_sev, .direction = "___") |>
  mutate(prev_sev = lag(last_sev)) |> ungroup()
risk <- grid |> filter(visit >= 2, visit <= pmin(last_visit + 1, 6)) |>
  mutate(stay = as.integer(visit <= ___))
```

(b) Fit a logistic model for `stay` on `prev_sev` and `arm`, then compute each participant's cumulative probability of remaining and the weights.

```{r}
#| eval: false
drop_model <- glm(stay ~ prev_sev + arm, family = binomial, data = risk)
risk <- risk |> mutate(p_stay = fitted(drop_model)) |>
  group_by(id) |> mutate(cum_p = ___(p_stay)) |> ungroup()
clear_w <- clear |> left_join(select(risk, id, visit, cum_p), by = c("id", "visit")) |>
  mutate(cum_p = ifelse(visit == 1, 1, cum_p), ipw = 1 / cum_p)
summary(clear_w$ipw)
```

(c) Fit unweighted and weighted logistic GEEs with an independence working correlation and compare the coefficients.

```{r}
#| eval: false
gee_unw <- geeglm(itch ~ week * arm, id = factor(id), data = clear_w,
                  family = binomial, corstr = "independence")
gee_ipw <- geeglm(itch ~ week * arm, id = factor(id), data = clear_w,
                  family = binomial, corstr = "independence", weights = ___)
cbind(unweighted = coef(gee_unw), ipw = coef(gee_ipw))
```

(d) In which direction does weighting move the placebo week slope? Is that the direction you would expect, given how dropout was generated?

(e) Why is an independence working correlation used? Why are the standard errors of the weighted fit only approximate?

## Independent exercises

### Exercise 7. The character-identifier trap (LO 7.3, 7.4)

Fit the CLEAR model of Exercise 3 with `id = id` (the character identifier) instead of `id = factor(id)`. Read the warning, compare the standard errors with those of Exercise 3 and explain what has gone wrong. Then check how many clusters `geeglm` believes there are in each fit. Write a one-line rule for your own analyses.

### Exercise 8. Categorical time in CLEAR (LO 7.4)

Fit a logistic GEE for `itch` with `week_f * arm` (a separate proportion for each arm at each scheduled week) and an exchangeable working correlation. Estimate the risk difference between arms at week 12 with a 95% CI and compare it with the linear-in-week model of Exercise 3. Which model would you prespecify for a trial, and why?

### Exercise 9. Clinics as clusters (LO 7.5)

The 360 WALK participants were recruited at 8 clinics. Treat **clinic** as the cluster: sort the data by clinic, participant and month, and fit `sbp ~ visit_f * arm` with an independence working correlation and `id = clinic`. Compare the sandwich SE and the Mancl–DeRouen SE of `visit_f12:armEP` with those from Exercise 2 (participants as clusters, independence). What does the comparison tell you about inference with 8 clusters? Is clinic-level clustering the relevant source of correlation for the WALK treatment comparison?

### Exercise 10. Overdispersion and the model-based SE in DIARY (LO 7.3)

Fit the DIARY model of Exercise 4 with an independence working correlation. Compare the robust SE of `post:armActive` with (i) the model-based SE from `fit$geese$vbeta.naiv` and (ii) the SE from an ordinary `glm()` with `family = poisson` and the same offset. Explain the differences, referring to overdispersion and to the correlation within participants.
